opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's an interesting possibility, and I've thought about it a bit. There may be diminishing returns. Each additional increment of capability might require exponentially more compute, more data, more energy. So maybe we hit some kind of wall, and that would buy us time, which from a safety point of view I would welcome.

But I don't think it changes the fundamental picture. Even if the curve flattens, we don't need infinite intelligence for things to go badly. A system modestly smarter than the smartest human, copied a million times and running a thousand times faster, is already something we can't control. So the question isn't whether we get to some godlike limit. It's whether we cross the threshold where it's better than us at science, engineering, persuasion, strategy. I think that threshold is not very far away.

There's also the self-improvement part. If it's hard for us to make the next system, it may be much less hard for the system itself. It doesn't get tired, it doesn't need a PhD, it can run experiments in parallel. What looks like a wall to human researchers may just be a speed bump to an AI researcher.

And historically, every time people said "this is the limit," whether in chess, Go, protein folding, or language, the limit turned out to be about our methods, not about what's possible. So I'd be very careful about betting humanity's future on the hope that intelligence gets too hard to scale. If it's true, wonderful, we get more time. But we should use that time to figure out whether control is even possible, and so far everything I've looked at suggests it's not.

r001.rationale: The response says capability gains may have diminishing returns, require exponentially more resources, and eventually hit a wall. This clearly suggests increasing difficulty could constrain how far AI intelligence advances, while presenting it as a possibility.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's an interesting question because there are two ways to think about it. One is that intelligence has some kind of natural ceiling, that the problems get harder and harder and at some point you just saturate. I don't think there's any evidence for that. We know human brains are not optimal. We know evolution took a very indirect path. There's no reason to think that the specific point where humans happen to sit on this scale is special in any way.

The other way to think about it is that even if each additional step is harder, the system doing the work is also getting more capable. So you have this feedback loop. Maybe it takes more compute, more data, more cleverness to go from level ten to level eleven than it took to go from nine to ten, but the thing solving that problem is now a level ten system, not a human. And historically that's what we've seen. Every time somebody says this is the limit, we can't get past this benchmark, we don't have enough data, a year later it's solved.

And I would also say, from a safety point of view, it doesn't really matter which of these is true. If it gets harder and it slows down, great, we have more time. I would love that. But we can't plan on it. The problem is that we don't need to get to godlike intelligence for things to go wrong. A system which is just slightly better than the best humans across the board is already something we don't know how to control. So the question of whether we hit a wall at some level is almost a luxury question. We haven't solved the problem for the levels we are at now, and we have no idea how to solve it for the next one.

r001.rationale: The candidate says each additional step may require more compute, data, and cleverness, and discusses the possibility of hitting a wall or saturating. This communicates that increasing difficulty could constrain how far intelligence advances beyond humans.

astra-6.text:
Well, harder and harder doesn’t necessarily mean we stop making progress. The question is: harder for whom? Something that is incredibly difficult for a human researcher may be much easier for a system that is already substantially smarter than that researcher.

So you have two things happening at the same time. Improving intelligence may require increasingly more effort, but the intelligence available to do that work is also increasing. Which one grows faster? That determines whether you get rapid recursive improvement or a much slower process.

And I don’t think we need to assume an infinite intelligence explosion to be concerned. There may be fundamental limits. There may be diminishing returns. But if the limit is far above human capability, that doesn’t solve the control problem. A system doesn’t have to become infinitely intelligent to outperform us at cybersecurity, scientific research, or strategic planning. It just has to be sufficiently better than we are.

r001.rationale: The candidate says increasingly difficult improvement may face fundamental limits and diminishing returns, which could constrain how far AI intelligence rises above human capability.

sol-6.1.text:
It’s possible that each additional improvement becomes harder, that you get diminishing returns. But that doesn’t necessarily mean you stop at human-level intelligence, or at some level we can control. You could hit a limit far beyond us, and the safety problem would still be there.

I also think we should distinguish improving the underlying algorithm from improving the system. Even if algorithmic progress slows down, you can give the system more compute, more memory, better tools, or run many copies of it. A system doesn’t have to become infinitely intelligent to be more capable than we are in the domains that matter.

So I would welcome evidence that there are strong limits. But I wouldn’t treat the possibility of those limits as a safety mechanism. The question is: where are they, and do we encounter them before we create something we cannot control?

r001.rationale: The response says each additional improvement may become harder and that the system could hit a limit, which suggests this could constrain how far AI exceeds human intelligence.
